questions.stem: What happens to an enzyme at very high temperatures?

options.text: It is killed
It dissolves in the solution
It becomes more active indefinitely
It is denatured — the active site changes shape permanently

questions.explanation: Enzymes are denatured at high temperatures, not 'killed.' Enzymes are proteins, not living organisms, so they cannot be killed. Denaturation means the bonds maintaining the tertiary structure break, permanently changing the active site shape so the substrate can no longer fit. Using 'killed' in an exam would lose marks.

questions.stem: What do enzymes do to the activation energy of a reaction?

options.text: They increase the activation energy
They lower the activation energy
They provide energy for the reaction
They have no effect on activation energy

questions.explanation: Enzymes lower the activation energy required for a reaction to take place, making it easier for the reaction to occur at body temperature. They do NOT provide energy for the reaction — this is a common misconception. The activation energy is the minimum energy needed for a reaction to start.

questions.stem: Why is the induced-fit model considered more accurate than the lock-and-key model?

options.text: Because the enzyme is completely rigid and never changes shape
Because the active site changes shape slightly when the substrate binds, forming a tighter fit
Because the substrate changes shape to fit the enzyme
Because multiple substrates can fit into one active site at the same time

questions.explanation: In the induced-fit model, the active site is not a perfect fit initially. When the substrate binds, the active site changes shape slightly to fit more closely around the substrate, like a hand closing around a ball. This is more accurate than the lock-and-key model, which suggests the active site is a rigid, perfect fit.

questions.stem: Can enzymes catalyse synthesis (anabolic) reactions, or only breakdown (catabolic) reactions?

options.text: Enzymes do not catalyse any reactions — they provide energy instead
Enzymes only build up substances
Enzymes can catalyse both synthesis and breakdown reactions
Enzymes only break down substances

questions.explanation: Enzymes can catalyse both catabolic (breakdown) and anabolic (synthesis) reactions. For example, digestive enzymes break down food molecules, but other enzymes catalyse DNA replication, protein synthesis, and photosynthesis. Thinking enzymes only 'break down' substances is a common misconception.

questions.stem: What happens to enzyme activity at low temperatures (e.g., 5°C)?

options.text: There is no change in enzyme activity
The enzyme is denatured
Enzyme activity is reduced because molecules have less kinetic energy, but the enzyme is not denatured
The enzyme is destroyed permanently

questions.explanation: At low temperatures, enzyme activity is reduced because both enzyme and substrate molecules have less kinetic energy, resulting in fewer collisions and fewer enzyme-substrate complexes per unit time. Crucially, the enzyme is NOT denatured — activity will recover if the temperature increases. Denaturation only occurs at high temperatures or extreme pH.

questions.stem: Why does the rate of enzyme activity increase as temperature rises from 10°C to 37°C?

options.text: The enzyme's active site gets larger
The substrate changes shape to fit the enzyme better
More enzyme molecules are produced
Molecules have more kinetic energy, leading to more frequent successful collisions and more enzyme-substrate complexes formed per unit time

questions.explanation: As temperature increases, both enzyme and substrate molecules gain more kinetic energy, so they move faster and collide more frequently. More collisions means more enzyme-substrate complexes form per unit time, increasing the rate of reaction. This continues until the optimum temperature is reached.

questions.stem: What is Vmax?

options.text: The maximum concentration of enzyme in a solution
The maximum pH at which an enzyme functions
The maximum temperature at which an enzyme works
The maximum rate of reaction when all active sites are saturated with substrate

questions.explanation: Vmax is the maximum rate of reaction achieved when all enzyme active sites are occupied (saturated) with substrate. At Vmax, increasing substrate concentration further has no effect on the rate because there are no free active sites available. To increase the rate beyond Vmax, more enzyme would be needed.

questions.stem: Where does a competitive inhibitor bind?

options.text: To the substrate molecule
To the product molecule
To an allosteric site away from the active site
To the active site of the enzyme

questions.explanation: A competitive inhibitor has a similar shape to the substrate and binds directly to the active site, competing with the substrate for access. This prevents the substrate from entering the active site. Competitive inhibition can be overcome by increasing the substrate concentration.

questions.stem: Where does a non-competitive inhibitor bind?

options.text: Nowhere — it works by lowering the temperature
To the substrate, preventing it from reaching the enzyme
To the active site of the enzyme
To an allosteric site, changing the shape of the active site

questions.explanation: A non-competitive inhibitor binds to an allosteric site (a site on the enzyme that is not the active site). This causes the active site to change shape, so the substrate can no longer bind. Non-competitive inhibition CANNOT be overcome by increasing substrate concentration.

questions.stem: Can competitive inhibition be overcome by increasing substrate concentration?

options.text: No — competitive inhibition is always permanent
No — only non-competitive inhibition can be overcome this way
Yes — more substrate molecules outcompete the inhibitor for the active site
Yes — but only if the enzyme is denatured first

questions.explanation: Competitive inhibition CAN be overcome by increasing substrate concentration. Since the inhibitor and substrate compete for the same active site, adding more substrate increases the probability that substrate molecules will bind to the active site instead of the inhibitor. Non-competitive inhibition cannot be overcome this way.

questions.stem: How does extreme pH affect enzyme activity?

options.text: It denatures the enzyme by breaking ionic and hydrogen bonds that maintain the tertiary structure
It only affects the substrate, not the enzyme
It has no effect on enzyme activity
It kills the enzyme

questions.explanation: Extreme pH values (too acidic or too alkaline) disrupt the ionic bonds and hydrogen bonds that maintain the enzyme's tertiary structure. This changes the shape of the active site, so the substrate can no longer bind — the enzyme is denatured. Remember: enzymes are denatured, not 'killed,' since they are not alive.

questions.stem: What is an enzyme-substrate complex?

options.text: The temporary structure formed when a substrate binds to the enzyme's active site
The product of the enzyme-catalysed reaction
A permanently bonded enzyme and substrate that cannot separate
An enzyme that has been denatured by its substrate

questions.explanation: An enzyme-substrate complex is the temporary structure formed when the substrate binds to the enzyme's active site. The reaction then takes place, products are released, and the enzyme is free to bind to another substrate molecule. The enzyme is not changed or used up in the reaction.

questions.stem: Why is each enzyme specific to a particular substrate?

options.text: Because enzymes can only work at one temperature
Because enzymes are made of the same substrate they catalyse
Because the shape of the active site is complementary to the shape of a specific substrate
Because all enzymes have the same active site shape

questions.explanation: Each enzyme has a uniquely shaped active site that is complementary to the shape of its specific substrate (like a lock and key). The active site shape is determined by the precise folding of the protein (tertiary structure), which depends on the amino acid sequence (primary structure).

questions.stem: What is the optimum temperature for most human enzymes?
questions.explanation: Most human enzymes have an optimum temperature of approximately 37°C (body temperature). Above this, the rate of denaturation exceeds the increase in kinetic energy, so the overall rate decreases. Different organisms have enzymes with different optima — thermophilic bacteria have enzymes that work best above 70°C.

questions.stem: Is enzyme denaturation usually reversible or irreversible?

options.text: Always reversible — the enzyme will return to its original shape
Reversible only if the enzyme is placed in acid
Always irreversible at any temperature
Usually irreversible — once the tertiary structure is disrupted, it cannot refold correctly

questions.explanation: Denaturation caused by high temperatures is usually irreversible because the disruption of the tertiary structure is too severe for the protein to refold correctly. However, mild denaturation (e.g., slight temperature increase) may sometimes be reversed. Low temperatures do not cause denaturation — they just slow enzyme activity.

questions.stem: If you double the enzyme concentration (with excess substrate), what happens to the rate of reaction?

options.text: The rate doubles
The rate halves
The enzyme becomes denatured
The rate stays the same

questions.explanation: If substrate is in excess, doubling the enzyme concentration doubles the number of active sites available, so twice as many enzyme-substrate complexes can form per unit time, doubling the rate of reaction. This is a directly proportional relationship (when substrate is not limiting).

questions.stem: What is the role of pepsin in the digestive system?

options.text: It breaks down fats into fatty acids and glycerol
It breaks down cellulose in the large intestine
It breaks down starch into maltose in the mouth
It breaks down proteins into smaller peptides in the stomach at pH 2

questions.explanation: Pepsin is a protease enzyme that works in the stomach, breaking down proteins into smaller peptides. It has an optimum pH of about 2 (very acidic), which is maintained by hydrochloric acid secreted by the stomach lining. Amylase breaks down starch; lipase breaks down fats.

questions.stem: Why does increasing substrate concentration eventually stop increasing the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction?

options.text: All enzyme active sites become saturated — there are no free active sites for additional substrate
The substrate starts to inhibit the enzyme
The temperature of the reaction decreases
The enzyme becomes denatured by the excess substrate

questions.explanation: At high substrate concentrations, all enzyme active sites are occupied (saturated), so adding more substrate has no effect — there are no free active sites available. The rate plateaus at Vmax. To increase the rate further, you would need to add more enzyme molecules.

questions.stem: Which graph best represents the effect of temperature on enzyme activity?

options.text: A horizontal flat line showing no change
A curve that increases to a peak (optimum) and then decreases sharply
A curve that decreases continuously as temperature increases
A straight line increasing continuously with temperature

questions.explanation: Enzyme activity increases with temperature (due to increased kinetic energy and collisions) up to the optimum temperature, then decreases sharply as the enzyme becomes denatured. This creates a characteristic curve with a peak — not a straight line or a continuously increasing curve.

questions.stem: What does it mean when we say enzymes are biological catalysts?

options.text: They are inorganic substances that speed up reactions
They are proteins produced by living organisms that speed up chemical reactions without being used up
They are substances that slow down chemical reactions
They are living cells that carry out reactions

questions.explanation: Enzymes are biological catalysts — they are proteins made by living organisms that speed up the rate of chemical reactions without being used up or changed themselves. They can be reused many times. A catalyst lowers the activation energy needed for a reaction to occur.

questions.stem: A student writes: 'The enzyme worked faster because there was a higher amount of substrate.' Why might this lose marks?

options.text: Because the statement is completely wrong
Because substrate has no effect on enzyme rate
Because enzymes do not work with substrates
Because 'amount' is imprecise — the student should say 'concentration of substrate'

questions.explanation: Using 'amount' instead of 'concentration' is a common exam mistake. 'Amount' is vague — it could mean mass, volume, or number of molecules. 'Concentration' specifically refers to the quantity of substrate per unit volume, which is what affects the rate of reaction. Precise scientific terminology is essential.

questions.stem: Which of these statements about enzymes is correct?

options.text: Each enzyme can catalyse many different types of reaction
Enzymes increase the activation energy of a reaction
Enzymes are used up during the reaction they catalyse
Enzymes can be reused because they are not changed by the reaction

questions.explanation: Enzymes are not used up or permanently changed during a reaction. After the products are released, the enzyme's active site is free to accept another substrate molecule. This means one enzyme molecule can catalyse many reactions. Enzymes are also specific — each enzyme typically catalyses one type of reaction.

questions.stem: What is the effect of a non-competitive inhibitor on Vmax?

options.text: Vmax increases
Vmax decreases because fewer functional active sites are available
Vmax is not affected by any type of inhibitor
Vmax stays the same, but the reaction takes longer to reach it

questions.explanation: Non-competitive inhibitors reduce Vmax because they permanently change the shape of some enzyme active sites (regardless of substrate concentration), effectively reducing the number of functional enzyme molecules. With competitive inhibition, Vmax can still be reached if enough substrate is added to outcompete the inhibitor.

questions.stem: What is the optimum pH for most enzymes in the small intestine?

options.text: pH 7-8 (neutral to slightly alkaline)
pH 14 (strongly alkaline)
pH 5 (mildly acidic)
pH 2 (strongly acidic)

questions.explanation: Enzymes in the small intestine (such as pancreatic lipase, trypsin, and amylase) work best at around pH 7-8 (neutral to slightly alkaline). Bile from the liver neutralises the acidic chyme from the stomach, creating the correct pH. In contrast, pepsin in the stomach works best at pH 2.

questions.stem: Why are enzymes described as having a 'complementary' shape to their substrate?

options.text: The active site of the enzyme has a shape that fits the substrate precisely, like a jigsaw piece
The enzyme and substrate are made of the same molecule
The substrate is always smaller than the enzyme
The enzyme and substrate have identical shapes

questions.explanation: The active site of an enzyme has a shape that is complementary (fits together) with the shape of the substrate — they are not identical but fit together precisely. This is why enzymes are specific: only substrates with the correct shape can fit into the active site and form an enzyme-substrate complex.

questions.stem: What happens to the rate of reaction at the optimum temperature?

options.text: The enzyme is denatured
The rate is zero because all substrate has been used up
The rate is at its lowest
The rate is at its maximum — the balance between kinetic energy and denaturation is optimal

questions.explanation: At the optimum temperature, the rate of reaction is at its maximum. Below this temperature, there is not enough kinetic energy for maximum collisions. Above it, denaturation begins to reduce the number of functional enzymes faster than the increased kinetic energy can compensate.

questions.stem: Immobilised enzymes are used in industry. What is one advantage of immobilising enzymes?

options.text: The enzyme can be easily recovered and reused, reducing costs
The enzyme works faster when immobilised
The enzyme becomes permanently denatured
The enzyme no longer needs a substrate

questions.explanation: Immobilised enzymes are attached to an insoluble material (such as alginate beads). This allows them to be easily separated from the products and reused, reducing costs. It also means the product is not contaminated with the enzyme. Immobilisation may slightly reduce activity but offers practical advantages.

questions.stem: What is the role of amylase?

options.text: To break down fats into fatty acids and glycerol
To break down cellulose into glucose
To break down proteins into amino acids
To break down starch into maltose

questions.explanation: Amylase is a carbohydrase enzyme that breaks down starch into the disaccharide maltose. It is produced in the salivary glands (salivary amylase) and the pancreas (pancreatic amylase). Proteases break down proteins; lipase breaks down fats.

questions.stem: In an experiment, enzyme activity is measured at 20°C, 30°C, 40°C, 50°C, and 60°C. The highest activity is at 40°C and it drops to almost zero at 60°C. Why is activity almost zero at 60°C?

options.text: The reaction has already reached completion
The molecules are moving too fast for the enzyme to catch
The substrate has evaporated at 60°C
The enzyme has been denatured — the bonds maintaining the tertiary structure have broken, changing the active site shape

questions.explanation: At 60°C, the enzyme is denatured. The high temperature has broken the hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, and other interactions that maintain the enzyme's tertiary structure. The active site shape has changed, so the substrate can no longer bind and form enzyme-substrate complexes. This is usually irreversible.

questions.stem: What is the difference between intracellular and extracellular enzymes?

options.text: There is no difference — all enzymes work inside cells
Only extracellular enzymes are specific to their substrate
Intracellular enzymes work inside cells; extracellular enzymes are secreted and work outside cells
Intracellular enzymes are proteins; extracellular enzymes are lipids

questions.explanation: Intracellular enzymes catalyse reactions within the cell (e.g., catalase breaking down hydrogen peroxide, enzymes of respiration). Extracellular enzymes are secreted out of cells to work outside (e.g., digestive enzymes like amylase, protease, and lipase). Both types are proteins and both are substrate-specific.

questions.stem: What is the effect of competitive inhibition on the Km of an enzyme?

options.text: Km stays the same
Km becomes zero
Km decreases
Km increases — more substrate is needed to reach half-Vmax because the inhibitor is competing

questions.explanation: Competitive inhibition increases the apparent Km (the substrate concentration needed to reach half-Vmax). This is because the inhibitor competes with the substrate for the active site, so a higher substrate concentration is needed to achieve the same rate. However, Vmax can still be reached with enough substrate.

questions.stem: Why does lipase work more efficiently when bile salts are present?

options.text: Bile emulsifies fats into smaller droplets, increasing the surface area for lipase to act on
Bile is an enzyme that helps lipase
Bile directly activates lipase by changing its active site
Bile changes the pH to the optimum for lipase

questions.explanation: Bile salts emulsify fats — they break large fat globules into smaller droplets, increasing the total surface area available for lipase to act on. This increases the rate of fat digestion. Importantly, bile is NOT an enzyme — it does not catalyse any chemical reaction. It only provides physical breakdown.

questions.stem: What happens to the products after an enzyme-catalysed reaction?

options.text: The enzyme breaks down along with the products
The products are stored inside the enzyme
The products are released from the active site, and the enzyme is free to catalyse another reaction
The products remain permanently attached to the enzyme

questions.explanation: After the reaction occurs, the products no longer fit the active site (their shape has changed from the substrate) and are released. The enzyme is unchanged and its active site is now free to bind another substrate molecule. This is why enzymes can be used repeatedly.

questions.stem: A student plots a graph showing reaction rate against substrate concentration with and without a competitive inhibitor. How do the two curves compare?

options.text: Both curves are identical
The inhibited curve shows a higher rate at all substrate concentrations
Both curves reach the same Vmax, but the inhibited curve reaches it at a higher substrate concentration
The inhibited curve has a lower Vmax and reaches it at the same substrate concentration

questions.explanation: With competitive inhibition, Vmax remains the same (it can be reached by adding enough substrate to outcompete the inhibitor), but the curve is shifted to the right — a higher substrate concentration is needed to reach each rate. The apparent Km is increased.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly explains why each enzyme has a specific optimum pH?

options.text: The substrate can only exist at one specific pH
At the optimum pH, the ionic and hydrogen bonds maintaining the active site shape are at their most stable, ensuring maximum enzyme-substrate binding
pH has no real effect on enzymes — the optimum pH is determined by the substrate
The enzyme only dissolves at its optimum pH

questions.explanation: Each enzyme has a specific optimum pH where the ionic and hydrogen bonds that maintain its tertiary structure (and therefore the shape of the active site) are most stable. Changes in pH alter the charges on amino acid R-groups, disrupting these bonds and changing the active site shape, reducing enzyme activity.
